name: Europa Clipper
primaryInstruments: Radar for Europa Assessment and Sounding: Ocean to Near-surface (REASON)
Interior Characterization of Europa using Magnetometry (ICEMAG)
keyEngineeringChallenge: Surviving Jupiter's intense radiation environment while generating sufficient electrical power at 5.2 AU using solar panels spanning over 30 meters.
educationalComparison: Notice how Europa Clipper carries 2,750 kg of fuel (nearly half its total launch weight!) just to decelerate and perform flybys. Generating power at 5.2 AU required the largest solar arrays ever built for a planetary mission.

name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)
powerSystem: Single 3.2m x 4.3m Solar Array (1850W) + Li-ion Battery
keyEngineeringChallenge: Thermal extremes (120°C to -230°C) and massive downlink volume: LRO returns hundreds of terabits of imagery per year using a high-rate Ka-band link.
educationalComparison: LRO shows how Ka-band high-gain communications enable high-resolution surface mapping. Without Ka-band, its 0.5-meter resolution imagery would take decades to downlink.

name: MAVEN (Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN)
powerSystem: Two 2.3m x 1.9m Solar Wings (1135W at Earth, ~490W at Mars)
primaryInstruments: Neutral Gas and Ion Mass Spectrometer (NGIMS)
keyEngineeringChallenge: Balancing solar wing area against high atmospheric drag during 'deep dip' campaigns into Mars's upper atmosphere.
educationalComparison: MAVEN illustrates the inverse-square law of solar power: its panels generated 1,135W at launch near Earth, but only 490W once arriving at Mars at 1.52 AU.

name: Juno
powerSystem: Three 9m Solar Wings (14,000W at Earth, ~450W at Jupiter)
keyEngineeringChallenge: First mission to Jupiter powered by solar instead of nuclear RTGs, housed inside a 1-centimeter-thick titanium radiation vault.
educationalComparison: Juno used an armored titanium vault weighing nearly 200 kg just to shield its computer from Jupiter's radiation belts. Without it, the electronics would have fried in weeks.
